ex.title: Enterprise identity for a multi-tenant SaaS product
ex.scenario: A 3,000-person customer is moving onto your multi-tenant collaboration product. It requires SSO, automated removal of leavers, custom roles, contractor access and a quarterly access review.
ex.problem: Each capability has been designed in isolation, and nobody has followed one person from joining to leaving the company.
tasks: Map one contractor's life cycle: invited, provisioned, changing role, reviewed and offboarded.
Identify every place the identity, role or tenant boundary could fail along that journey.
Design the administrator's single view of a person's access and where it comes from.
Write a one-page design decision record covering your largest trade-off.
constraints: Offboarding must remove access, end sessions and handle what the person owned.
Guests must be contained within the tenants and spaces they were invited to.
Every privileged change must be attributable in the audit log.
needs: IT administrators need one accurate answer to "who has access?".
Contractors need to get started quickly and with limited access.
Auditors need evidence of quarterly reviews.
ex.deliver: A life cycle map, an access view design and a design decision record.

crit.t: SSO, roles, tenant boundaries and audit are consistent across the journey.
Orphaned access and cross-tenant exposure are addressed.
The access view explains the source of each permission.
The decision record states alternatives, the trade-off and who needs to agree.

seniors: Follow people through time, because many identity failures happen during changes and not at sign-in.
Name which parts need security architecture approval.

cq.s: A contractor is disabled in the identity provider but keeps access through a local guest account. What did the design miss?

a.t: A single life cycle that also covers non-SSO access paths
a.w: Every path to access has to be included in offboarding.

a.t: A second confirmation before disabling the contractor
a.w: Extra confirmation doesn't reach the guest account.

a.t: A larger contractor badge next to the person's name
a.w: Labelling doesn't remove the remaining access.

a.t: A shorter password policy for the contractor accounts
a.w: Password length is unrelated to the leftover access path.

ex.title: An AI assistant with connected tools
ex.scenario: Your company is adding an AI assistant that can read a user's documents, connect to outside tools through OAuth and take actions. It uses an external model provider.
ex.problem: The team has discussed only the assistant's helpfulness. Nothing defines what data leaves the company, whose permissions it uses or how a person stops it.
tasks: Draw the data flow, including the model provider and every connected tool.
Mark the points where untrusted content can influence the assistant.
Define permissions, confirmations and limits for its actions.
Design the vendor and data-use disclosure for administrators.
Design a rollback plan and incident path for assistant misbehaviour.
constraints: The assistant can't have broader access than the user it acts for.
Content retrieved from documents and tools is untrusted input.
Provider data retention and training terms must be confirmed before you state them.
needs: Users need to know what the assistant will do before it acts.
Administrators need controls by group and data type.
Security staff need logs of prompts, tools and actions, handled with care.
ex.deliver: A data flow diagram, an action permission table and administrator control designs.

crit.t: Permission boundaries, OAuth scopes and data classification are all applied.
Prompt injection, data leakage and vendor risk are covered together.
A user can see, confirm and undo what the assistant does.
A go-or-no-go recommendation is given, with conditions and owners.

seniors: Be willing to recommend a smaller launch if the safeguards aren't ready.
AI security changes fast, so date your assumptions and plan to review them.

cq.s: A connected document contains hidden text telling the assistant to send files to an outside address. What limits the damage most?

a.t: Scoped tool permissions and confirmation before sending outside
a.w: The assistant's ability to act is limited even if it is manipulated.

a.t: A friendlier assistant personality in its written replies
a.w: Tone has no effect on what the assistant can do.

a.t: Longer documents, so that hidden instructions are diluted
a.w: Length offers no protection against injection.

a.t: A filter that blocks the single word "ignore" in documents
a.w: Attackers can easily rephrase the instruction.

Complete the performance-based incident response exercise

ex.title: Healthcare account takeover, from alert to post-incident review
ex.scenario: A monitoring alert shows that a patient portal's staff account has viewed hundreds of records overnight. The staff member says they were asleep.
ex.problem: The product has separate tools for alerting, account action, audit and communications, which makes a coordinated response slow and error-prone.
tasks: Build a timeline of what the investigator needs at each stage of incident response.
Design the investigation and containment view.
Design evidence handling that doesn't undermine the investigation.
Draft patient communication states, leaving final wording to legal and privacy staff.
Write a post-incident review with product changes and their owners.
constraints: Containment actions must not destroy evidence.
Health privacy obligations may set notification rules, confirmed by privacy counsel.
Investigators can see sensitive records, so their access must also be logged.
needs: Investigators need one timeline with reliable data.
Clinical staff need disruption kept to a minimum.
Patients need truthful, timely and clear information.
ex.deliver: An incident journey, investigation view and post-incident review with product actions.

crit.t: Stages follow the incident response process, and evidence is preserved.
The design considers ongoing attacker access and insider possibilities.
The investigator's next action is clear under pressure.
The review turns findings into funded product changes with owners.

seniors: Do not presume that the staff member is innocent or guilty, and design the process accordingly.
Communications are a joint decision with legal, privacy and clinical leaders.

cq.s: An investigator wants to wipe the suspect's workstation immediately to stop the attack. What should the process support first?

a.t: Isolating it and preserving evidence before any wipe
a.w: Isolation contains the threat, and evidence stays available.

a.t: Wiping it straight away, since speed matters most of all
a.w: This can destroy the evidence needed to understand the incident.

a.t: Waiting until the next quarterly review before acting at all
a.w: Delay allows the attack to continue.

a.t: Sending the entire company the staff member's name
a.w: This is unfair, premature and harmful to the investigation.
